title: What meditation research shows
hook: a 2014 review of 47 trials found moderate help for anxiety, depression and pain (Goyal et al., JAMA)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the wandering mind, nearly half the time somewhere else. Your line was where is it now. Where did yours go? Day three hundred five.
screen: `THE WANDERING MIND — WHERE IS IT NOW?`

segments.voice: If you typed does meditation work into a search bar, you'd get two kinds of answers. One camp says it changes everything: stress, sleep, focus, relationships, your whole brain. The other camp rolls its eyes: it's sitting still, and the rest is marketing. Both sound confident. Neither usually tells you where their confidence comes from. So instead of one study, or one enthusiast, let's look at what happens when careful researchers gather up dozens of trials at once and ask what holds. Today: what meditation research shows.
screen: `IT CHANGES EVERYTHING.` → `IT'S JUST SITTING STILL.` → `WHAT HOLDS?`

segments.voice: In 2014 a team led by Madhav Goyal at Johns Hopkins published a review in JAMA Internal Medicine. A review like this doesn't run a new experiment. It collects the existing ones and weighs them together. They started from thousands of published papers and kept only randomized trials, where people were assigned by chance, and only trials with an active comparison group, something like a health education class, so that attention and hope were matched. Remember yesterday's question: compared to what? That was the whole point. Forty-seven trials made the cut, with about thirty-five hundred people. Here's what they found. Mindfulness meditation programs, usually around eight weeks long, showed moderate evidence of improving anxiety, depression and pain. Moderate is a technical word here: it describes how confident the reviewers were, and the size of the improvements was small to moderate. For stress and quality of life, the evidence was low. For attention, sleep, mood and weight, it was low or not enough to say. And when meditation was compared with other active treatments, like exercise, medication or therapy, there was no evidence it did better. So that's the honest shape. Not a miracle. Not nothing. A real, modest help for some real problems, about as solid as many things doctors recommend, and no substitute for care when you need it. Many traditions on this path would say that isn't why they sit anyway. That's fair too. But if someone asks you whether the science says meditation helps, now you have a true answer. Moderate, and real.
screen: `GOYAL ET AL., JAMA INTERNAL MEDICINE, 2014.` · `47 TRIALS, ACTIVE COMPARISONS.` · `ANXIETY, DEPRESSION, PAIN: MODERATE.` · `NOT BETTER THAN OTHER TREATMENTS.` · then, large: `MODERATE, AND REAL.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, take a quick reading: on a scale of one to ten, how settled do you feel right now? Just a number. Then sit with the breath, the way we have all year, noticing and coming back. When the bell rings, you'll take the reading again. No right answer. You're gathering one small, honest data point. The bell holds the time.
What meditation research shows. A 2014 review of 47 trials found moderate evidence that meditation programs ease anxiety, depression and pain. Today's word.
Your line: moderate, and real. After any sitting today, notice how you feel, and compare it honestly to before. Day three hundred five.

howItsDone: Clinicians sometimes suggest mindfulness programs, often eight weeks long, alongside other care for anxiety, depression or chronic pain, drawing on reviews like Goyal et al.

options: randomized trials with an active comparison group.
the ones with the biggest headlines.
fork.reveal: Goyal's team kept only randomized trials against active controls, like a health education class.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation either works or it's hype.
what it means: moderate evidence of modest help for anxiety, depression and pain.
what a scholar hears: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 RCTs with active controls; no advantage over other active treatments.

notes: The outline says 'JAMA'; the journal is JAMA Internal Medicine. The script uses the full name; the outline could be updated.

Goyal et al. (2014): 47 trials, 3,515 participants; moderate-strength evidence for anxiety, depression and pain (mindfulness programs); low for stress/distress and mental-health quality of life; low or insufficient for positive mood, attention, substance use, eating, sleep, weight; no evidence of superiority to active treatments. Confirm.
